questions.q: Which scipy.optimize.minimize method is specifically designed to handle general nonlinear equality and inequality constraints?
options: Nelder-Mead
BFGS
SLSQP
linprog
questions.explain: SLSQP (Sequential Least Squares Programming) is designed for problems with general equality and inequality constraints, unlike plain BFGS (unconstrained) or Nelder-Mead (derivative-free, unconstrained).

questions.q: What is the main benefit of supplying an analytic gradient via the `jac` argument instead of relying on the solver's default finite-difference approximation?
options: It makes the problem convex
It guarantees the global optimum will be found
It improves both convergence speed and numerical accuracy, especially for objectives sensitive to floating-point cancellation
It removes the need for any constraints
questions.explain: Finite-difference gradients are both slower to compute and more prone to numerical error. Supplying the exact analytic gradient avoids this approximation error and typically speeds convergence.

questions.q: Why does maximizing the Sharpe ratio need extra caution compared to minimizing portfolio variance?
options: Because the Sharpe ratio objective is generally nonconvex, so the local minimum found may not be the global optimum
Because Sharpe ratio maximization has no gradient
Because variance minimization always ignores expected returns
Because Sharpe ratio maximization cannot be coded in Python
questions.explain: Unlike the convex minimum-variance QP, Sharpe-ratio maximization is not guaranteed convex, so Lesson 26's local-equals-global guarantee doesn't automatically apply, and extra care (like multi-start) is warranted.

questions.q: What problem does a 'multi-start' optimization strategy address?
options: Poor internet connectivity during optimization
The risk that a nonconvex objective's single optimization run converges to a local, non-global optimum
The need to use multiple programming languages
Ensuring constraints are always linear
questions.explain: Multi-start reruns the optimization from several different starting points and keeps the best result, guarding against a nonconvex objective trapping the solver in a mediocre local minimum.

questions.q: Why can poor variable scaling (e.g., mixing variables on wildly different numeric scales) hurt an optimizer's convergence?
options: It has no effect on convergence
It only affects linear programs, never quadratic ones
It inflates the effective condition number of the problem, slowing or stalling gradient-based convergence
It always causes the objective function to become negative
questions.explain: When variables have very different natural scales, the Hessian's condition number worsens, making the optimization landscape elongated and harder for gradient-based methods to navigate efficiently.
